12317-two-little-knights-of-kentucky:
Two Little Knights of Kentucky is a children book about the Little Colonel circle, dedicated to Margaret, Albion, Mary, Helen, Lura, Rose, William, and George. The story belongs to Annie Fellows Johnston Little Colonel series, set in Lloydsborough, Kentucky.

Chapters open on the coldest Saint Valentine eve Kentucky had known in twenty years, with two tramps and a bear. Later chapters bring Ginger and the boys, a valentine party, a fire and a plan, Jonesy benefit, and the Little Colonel two rescues. A mid-book scene has Virginia admire pretty articles made from almost nothing, including a helmet with nodding plumes. The book mixes play, rescue, and Southern manners for young readers.
13933-in-old-kentucky:
Edward Marshall and Charles T. Dazey turned Dazey's play In Old Kentucky into a 1910 novel of the Bluegrass and the mountains. Illustrations by Clarence Rowe picture a stranger breaking through undergrowth about a pool and a leap beyond a blazing barrier. Mountain folk, horse lovers, and Bluegrass gentry meet and clash.

A mountain girl gazes at a wondrous view and declares learning could not make her love it more. Feuds, races, and romances drive the plot, in the manner of the stage original. The novel keeps the play's broad humour and sentiment. It captures Kentucky local colour as popular audiences loved it. Readers of regional romance will enjoy its pace.
15521-the-adventures-of-prickly-porky:
Thornton W. Burgess published this bedtime story book in Boston in 1916, with Little, Brown, illustrated by Harrison Cady. It belongs to his Bedtime Story-Books, beside the Old Mother West Wind series. A frontispiece shows a cry for news of Peter Rabbit, setting the woodland cast in motion.

Twenty-three chapters follow Prickly Porky, the porcupine stranger from the north, as he makes friends, nearly chokes, and meets Jimmy Skunk, Unc' Billy Possum, Reddy Fox, and Old Granny Fox. Peter Rabbit tells his story many times, a plot frightens Old Man Coyote, and Buster Bear gives it all away. Burgess writes short, gentle chapters for young children, teaching animal lore through talk, trouble, and friendship in the Green Forest.
19477-the-young-trailers-a-story-of-earl:
Joseph A. Altsheler wrote this tale of early Kentucky, published in the early nineteen hundreds. Two boys, Henry and Paul, push into unknown woods, lose their way, explore a great cave by torchlight, and face a siege that tests their courage and their bond.

Chapters on haunted forests, giant bones, and a wild turkey's call give the frontier its wonder as well as its danger. Altsheler wrote many such books for boys, and this one shows his formula at its best: young heroes learning woodcraft, loyalty, and duty on the edge of settlement.
20649-oomphel-in-the-sky:
H. Beam Piper's Oomphel in the Sky is a science fiction story set on a colony world far from Earth. It opens with a communication screen snapping on. Harry Walsh, the news editor, looks out from his office in Bluelake, halfway across the continent, and wants to know how things are going.

The man he calls is deep in trouble with the planet's native peoples. Their word oomphel names the strange sky craft and goods they cannot explain. Piper, famous for his future histories, builds the tale on language, trade, and the clash of two worlds' ideas.
20719-under-the-country-sky:
Grace S. Richmond set her novel Under the Country Sky in a country town, among the people her heroine serves and loves. Richmond wrote warm stories of doctors, ministers, and their families in small places. Her heroine's patience with her neighbors is tested on every page.

She loved them all, the narrator explains, so it would go hard with her if she had to hate them. Love turned to hate is such a bitter product. But she had never found it so hard to be patient with them as now. Under that strain, the novel tests what small-town kindness costs the one who gives it.
21568-sweet-their-blood-and-sticky:
Albert R. Teichner's tale Sweet Their Blood and Sticky ran in Worlds of If in November 1961. A vast machine, hundreds of feet long, stands working alone in a desert. It can run on a thimbleful of earth or water, drawing all it needs from the land.

With its packing gear broken, the machine pours out a stream of pink-striped taffy. Once a whole desert of such devices fed a needful human race. Now the makers are gone, and something not human inherits the earth. Teichner builds a chill, strange tale from candy, dust, and four dimensions.
23327-lodusky:
Frances Hodgson Burnett set this tale among mountain folk in Tennessee in eighteen seventy seven. Lodusky, a slight young woman who earns her keep by writing, comes to a rough country dance with an older kinswoman, and the local folk eye the pair with keen interest.

The story moves through dances, games, and talk at mountain homes, where manners are plain and speech is blunt. Lodusky watches it all with bright eyes, while neighbours weigh her book learning against their own ways. Burnett uses the gap between the visiting writer and her hosts to draw a warm, close picture of mountain life and of a young woman finding her place in it.
23798-daniel-boone-the-pioneer-of-kentuc:
John S. C. Abbott published Daniel Boone, The Pioneer of Kentucky, in 1872, in the American Pioneers and Patriots series. Abbott opens by challenging the popular image of Boone as a crude frontiersman, nearly as wild as the bears he hunted and the Native peoples he confronted.

Abbott presents the opposite portrait instead: a mild man who never boasted, gentle in taste and bearing, who kept coarse speech and rude conduct out of his life. With that refinement went a boldness that seemed incapable of fear. Abbott's life follows Boone's wonderful career for young readers, presenting him as nature's gentleman on the frontier.
23882-gold-in-the-sky:
Alan E. Nourse published Gold in the Sky as a book-length novel in Amazing Science Fiction Stories in September 1958. Its cast is introduced at once. Greg Hunter is a test pilot happy only when his life hangs in the balance. Tom Hunter is a pioneer whose frontier hides in test tubes. Johnny Coombs is a prospector who returned from the asteroids too soon.

Against them stand Merrill Tawney, an industrialist seeking plunder beyond the stars, and Major Briarton, a government man whose creed is law and order. Chapters run from Trouble Times Two and Jupiter Equilateral through the Black Raider, the Haunted Ship, and the Sinister Bonanza to the Missing Asteroid and the Final Move. It is space adventure with gold at its heart.
2803-the-rise-of-david-levinsky:
Abraham Cahan wrote The Rise of David Levinsky as the life story of a Jewish immigrant who climbs from poverty to wealth in New York's garment trade. Levinsky arrives as a Talmud student from Russia, works his way through sweatshops and peddling, and slowly learns the business of cloaks and suits. The novel follows his rise alongside his hunger for learning, love, and respect.

Cahan sets Levinsky's success against what it costs him, since business skill never quite fills the place left by faith and feeling. Scenes of the Lower East Side, the shops, and the counting houses give the story its texture. It endures as an immigrant novel that refuses to treat wealth as a simple happy ending.
5661-a-son-of-the-gods-and-a-horseman-in:
Ambrose Bierce, who fought in the Civil War as a young soldier, pairs two short studies of war in this small volume, with an introduction by Morrow. The introduction presents Bierce as poet, critic, satirist, and writer of fables, and it stresses that his war writing comes from direct experience rather than distant report. Both tales are brief, sharp, and centered on single moments when a soldier must act.

Readers get war stripped of parade and speeches, told through choice, fear, and sudden fate. The value of the pair lies in its compression. A whole argument about courage and chance rides on one watch, one ride, and one shot. The spare prose leaves the moral weight to the reader rather than spelling it out.
6012-charlemont-or-the-pride-of-the-vill:
W. Gilmore Simms calls Charlemont a domestic legend founded on actual events of recent occurrence in Kentucky. However strange the facts may seem, and however they clash with supposed sensibilities of woman, Simms insists most were conclusively established by the record. He dedicates the tale and its sequel Beauchampe to James Hall of Cincinnati.

The epigraph warns that security in one's own strength breeds negligence, and negligence breeds unremedied ruin. Simms, a pioneer literary voice of the West, sets village pride against private passion. The novel follows Kentucky folk whose choices turn from confidence toward trouble.
6574-watchers-of-the-sky:
Alfred Noyes opens a verse trilogy on science with the watchers of the sky, from early star-gazers to the men who found laws in the heavens. His preface says the poem seeks the great moments when facts, long gathered, fell into a clear order, and changed how all folk thought. He does not try to cover all science, nor to build a new system in verse.

Instead, the torch passes from hand to hand through the years, each bearer adding light to the last. Noyes writes with a poet's eye for the human heat inside cold discovery, for doubt, toil, and sudden sight. Watchers of the Sky is a long poem about how star lore grew, step by step, into modern astronomy.
6612-myths-and-legends-of-our-own-land-v:
Along the Rocky Range, Skinner follows the hope of El Dorado that drew Spaniards and later mountain men west. Gold finds in California and Colorado gave fresh color to that old dream, and tales of phantom trains, lost souls, desert riders, and a Yellowstone tragedy grew from it. The range itself looms large, harsh and grand.

Navajo arrivals, a goddess of salt, a flood at Santa Fe, and a battle in the air fill the later tales. Skinner writes with a westerner's relish for tall tales and hard truth mixed. This seventh volume suits readers who like mountain lore, where gold, gods, and ghosts share the same high trail.
6630-curiosities-of-the-sky:
Garrett Serviss invites readers to look up and wonder, with chapters on star-clouds, star-streams, and the passing of constellations. Windows of absolute night, fires in the heavens, whirling nebulae, sun banners, and the zodiacal light all get their turn. Comets, meteors, fire-balls, and the wrecking of the moon add drama to the sky.

Serviss writes for the curious, not just for astronomers, with pictures of nebulae, clusters, and the Pleiades to aid the eye. His tone is one of awe mixed with clear fact. Curiosities of the Sky is a charming, early popular astronomy book, still fun for stargazers today.
6904-boy-scouts-in-an-airship-or-the-war:
Ned Nestor and Jimmie McGraw, Boy Scouts of the Wolf Patrol in New York City, meet a Secret Service man named Gates in a San Francisco room. Gates has come from Washington to brief Ned, who has taken on a hard and risky mission for the government in South America. The boys at first take Gates for a poser, then learn to heed his warning hand.

The tale moves from city streets to camp and sky, as the scouts face spies in their own camp and danger from above. Ralphson keeps the pace brisk, with secret orders, strange warnings, and young heroes asked to act like men. It is a boys adventure of loyalty, pluck, and flight.
a-son-of-the-gods-and-a-horseman-in-the-:
A Son of the Gods and A Horseman in the Sky gathers two Civil War stories by Ambrose Bierce, with an introduction by W C Morrow. Morrow stresses that Bierce was himself a boy soldier in the war, and calls these pieces studies of his many sided genius: poet, critic, satirist, and maker of fables. The volume appears as the fourth in a Western Classics series, with a frontispiece after a painting by Will Jenkins.

Each title names its scene. A horseman in the sky is a lookout posted above a valley, bound by duty to signal what he sees, even when the rider below is his own father. A son of the gods follows a young officer who rides out alone toward an enemy position to draw its fire. Bierce writes war as a test of nerve and obedience, with death close, plain, and rarely glorious.
boy-scouts-in-an-airship-or-the-warning-:
G. Harvey Ralphson's Boy Scouts in an Airship, or The Warning From the Sky, sends two Wolf Patrol scouts into a Secret Service adventure. Gates, a United States Secret Service man, enters a San Francisco hotel room with a warning hand raised, while Ned Nestor and Jimmie McGraw smile at what they take for detective posing.

Young Nestor has been engaged by the government for a hard and risky errand in South America, and Gates has come from Washington to post him on the details. From San Francisco the story moves toward airships, spies and the warning of the title. Ralphson writes briskly for boys, and readers who enjoy scouting tales mixed with early aviation and espionage will find it exciting.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kentucky:
Kentucky, between the Ohio and Mississippi rivers, gets a full survey here, from its land and climate to its laws and church life. This entry opens with geography: the eastern mountains, the rolling Bluegrass country, the limestone plateau, and Mammoth Cave, described as the world's largest natural cavern. It then turns to people, wealth, farming, mining, and transport.

General history leads into religion, with a long section on how the Catholic Church grew in the state. Kentucky law touching faith is covered too. Rules cover marriage and divorce, the sale of drink, wills and charitable bequests, and cemeteries, which paid no tax unless run for profit. Sources cited run from early state histories to a centenary volume on Kentucky Catholicity from 1884.
charlemont-or-the-pride-of-the-village-a:
Charlemont, or the Pride of the Village, a tale of Kentucky by W Gilmore Simms, is dedicated to James Hall of Cincinnati as a pioneer of western letters. Simms's advertisement warns readers plainly: the domestic legend that follows is founded on actual events of comparatively recent occurrence in Kentucky. However strange the facts appear, and however they conflict with what is supposed of women's sensibilities, he insists they are unquestionably true.

The events behind the tale form the famous Kentucky tragedy. Anna Cook is courted by the brilliant Charlemont of the title. She is betrayed. Her husband Beauchampe avenges her, and Simms reserved Beauchampe's story for a sequel of that name. Village pride, seduction, and duel culture drive the plot. Simms, the South's leading romancer, treats the case as national material: proof that American soil grew passions as operatic as any in Walter Scott.
curiosities-of-the-sky:
Garrett P. Serviss's Curiosities of the Sky is a popular astronomy book that tours the wonders visible overhead. Serviss, a well-known explainer of the heavens, takes up star-clouds and clusters, the slow migration of stars, and exploding nebulae. He also covers the banners of the sun, the zodiacal light, the aurora, comets, meteors and the riddle of the asteroids.

Chapters also weigh the great Mars problem of his day, the wrecking of the moon, and the passing of the constellations as the heavens change over ages. Illustrations show the Andromeda nebula, the Milky Way, the Pleiades, the Orion nebula and the corona. Each marvel is grounded in what telescopes actually revealed. The book suits curious readers who want the night sky made vivid without mathematics.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NSRP-BereaKY_NS: A fragment of a news article covers a rally of the National States Rights Party in Berea, Kentucky. The rally was marked by violence. The article blames the violence on 'outside agitators,' a phrase officials used often in those years. The party was a segregationist organization, and Berea was a small college town. The publication that carried the article is not identified, and the fragment does not preserve its date or its full account.
myths-and-legends-of-our-own-land-volume:
Charles M. Skinner rides west along the Rocky Range in this volume. A phantom train on Marshall Pass opens the contents. Lost souls' rivers and riders of the desert follow. A Yellowstone tragedy and a Santa Fe flood raise the peril.

Over the Divide tells of men still hunting El Dorado. Gold in California and Colorado kept that old dream alive. Miners braved hunger, sickness, and death for treasure caves. Navajo tales and a goddess of salt add Native depth. Skinner's West is vast and haunted, where tall tales grow as big as the peaks themselves.
podcast-dannyjones-xXq5o5rW_kY:
Breath coach Will Grant teaches how to fix the body using breath in episode 50 of the KONCRETE podcast with Danny Jones. Grant argues that most people breathe badly and pay for it in stress, pain, and poor sleep. His fix costs nothing and starts with the next inhale.

Grant explains simple breathing patterns and the body systems they affect. He shows how breath can calm nerves, steady the heart, and aid recovery after hard training. Jones tries the methods and asks how to build them into a daily routine. Breathless and curious listeners alike get air treated as real medicine.
podcast-joerogan-5jKEYKrA4kY:
Rogan reacts, in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience, to the Biden administration delaying the release of JFK assassination files. By law, the records were due to open in full, and each delay has fed public doubt about what the files hold.

The talk asks why, six decades on, agencies still fight to keep pages sealed. Rogan weighs the official reasons against the suspicion that delay itself is the message. He places the fight in a longer story of government secrecy. For listeners drawn to the Kennedy case, the segment captures the mood of the disclosure fight as it stood then.
podcast-joerogan-uFiR3nVtYKY:
Music producer Rick Rubin sits with Joe Rogan for episode 1881 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Rubin co-founded Def Jam and produced landmark records across rap, rock, and country. He is famous for stripping songs down to what matters and for his calm, zen-like style.

Rubin talks about creativity as a way of paying attention rather than forcing results. He shares how he helps artists trust their taste and cut away the rest. Rogan asks about fame, failure, and making art that lasts. Makers of any kind get a quiet master class in doing less, but better.
the-adventures-of-prickly-porky: Thornton W. Burgess wrote The Adventures of Prickly Porky for his Bedtime Story-Books, with art by Harrison Cady, printed at Boston by Little, Brown, and Company in 1916. Chapters listed open with Happy Jack Squirrel's find and a stranger from the North, then Prickly Porky making friends, Peter Rabbit's startling news, Jimmy Skunk's call, and Reddy Fox in misery.
the-rise-of-david-levinsky: Abraham Cahan is named as author on the edition header. The header gives the title of his novel. It gives a September 2001 release date. A later update followed in March 2009. Only that edition header is present on these pages. Its general notices appear with it. No part of the novel itself appears here. Nothing about David's rise can be told from these pages alone.
the-young-trailers-a-story-of-early-kent: Joseph A. Altsheler's The Young Trailers, copyrighted in 1907, is shown here through its dedication and contents. Altsheler dedicates the Kentucky story to Sydney, a young Kentuckian. Twelve chapters lead into the unknown wilderness. A haunted forest, giant bones, and a wild turkey's gobble appear. The escape and the primitive man close the list shown. The story chapters themselves do not appear in the pages present in this record.
two-little-knights-of-kentucky:
Two Little Knights of Kentucky opens its contents with Two Tramps and a Bear, then a valentine party, a fire, and Jonesy's benefit. A dedication names nine children of the author's circle. No author is named on the pages shown.

Chapter one sets the coldest Saint Valentine's eve Kentucky had known in twenty years. Snow in Lloydsborough Valley shows every rabbit track, and an ice-cutter's wagon creaks up from a pond. Inside the depot waiting-room, a red-hot stove cannot clear the frost from the window-panes. Two boys run up the track with skates in hand, half an hour before the five o'clock train. The knights' adventures begin in that frozen station.
watchers-of-the-sky:
Alfred Noyes wrote Watchers of the Sky as the first volume of The Torch-Bearers, a trilogy in verse on the story of scientific discovery. His prefatory note calls the volume complete in itself. It finds an epic unity in that story: a single torch of purpose and endeavor, passed from hand to hand through the centuries. His poem treats the great moments of the work. After long labor, the pioneers saw their gathered facts fall into a significant order.

Those moments, Noyes says, hold intense human interest. They belong to the creative imagination of poetry. He does not try to cover the whole field, or to build a new system of science in verse. The prologue pictures a night among the stars, when the new hundred-inch telescope was first tried.
